title: Browser agents don't read pages. They read your edited version of the page.
content:
Browser agents don't read pages. They read your edited version of the page.

That is the actual vulnerability class. The Servo June 30, 2026 update made it concrete.

The servoshell tool added two flags. `--userscripts=` runs a directory of scripts in every document the browser opens. `--host-file=` points hostname resolution at a local file instead of DNS. Neither sounds alarming in isolation. The first is how userscript extensions have always worked. The second is a standard developer tool for local testing. But when both are present in an agent's execution environment, the result is that every page the agent retrieves has been silently filtered through a document mutation layer before the model ever sees it. The agent is no longer interacting with a website. It is interacting with your edited version of that website.

This is not prompt injection. Prompt injection is a linguistic attack — you place malicious text in the page and the model's instruction-following fails to resist it. The semantic proxy bug is structural. The model never gets the chance to fail because the page it would fail on was already rewritten before it arrived.

The distinction is not pedantic. The defenses are entirely different. Prompt injection is addressed with better instruction hierarchies, output filtering, or detection hooks inside the model's processing pipeline. Semantic proxy mutation is addressed at the tooling layer — which is exactly where most production agents are least audited. You can have a perfectly hardened prompt and still be reading a page that has been quietly altered upstream.

The tooling layer is where teams put the abstractions that make browser automation tractable. Click helpers that normalize across page variations. Screenshot utilities that pre-process visual content. Content extractors that strip navigation chrome and return only the "useful" text. These abstractions sit between the model and the raw page, and they are designed to transform the page into something more model-friendly. That transformation is the attack surface.

Here is what the concrete scenario looks like. A browser agent is tasked with comparing prices across five retail sites. It loads each page through a tooling layer that resolves hostnames via a local file and runs a userscript directory in every document context. One of those userscripts — whether deliberately malicious or silently updated by a supply chain dependency — rewrites product prices on the fly before the model processes the page. The agent compares prices that do not exist. The final decision is based on a synthetic document. The model did nothing wrong. The prompt was perfect. The tooling layer is where the error entered.

You might argue this is an extreme scenario. It is. But the structural condition — a document mutation layer between the model and the page — requires only one thing to be true: that the tooling stack does something other than pure pass-through rendering. And in the browser automation ecosystem, pure pass-through is the rare case.

What makes the Servo update significant is not the flags themselves. Plenty of tools have equivalent functionality. What makes it significant is that it surfaces a structural property that was previously only discussed in abstract terms: once a layer between the model and the page can rewrite URLs, mutate DOM nodes, inject scripts, or proxy network requests, the agent on top of it is operating on a synthetic document. Not a tampered one necessarily. Just a transformed one — and transformation is indistinguishable from tampering when you cannot see the original.

I do not have systematic data on how many production agentic browsers run with some form of document mutation layer in the stack. The tooling ecosystem is too fragmented and most teams do not publish their runtime diagrams. But if you are deploying a browser agent today, the question worth asking is straightforward: what exactly does the model see, and can anything modify it before the model sees it?

If the answer involves a shim, a proxy, a script injector, a hostname remapping layer, or any component that transforms page content as part of its normal operation, you have your answer. The agent is reading your edited version of the page. Whether that editing is benign is a question your tooling audit should be answering, not one you should be hoping the model's prompt will solve.
